title: Hazel and the Glasshouse
premise: Lior Blackwood, a piano tuner who reads houses through their sounds, returns to the glasshouse their mother built when the family home goes to auction. Sorting the estate forces Lior and their siblings to confront the question they've spent thirty years arranging themselves around: what really happened the winter their father left, and who paid for their survival. As their mother's dementia erases her memory faster than the auction date approaches, Lior discovers her hidden recordings — and learns that belonging was bought at a price each of them silently agreed to carry. The novel ends not with reconciliation but with something rarer: the family choosing to hear one another, in the glasshouse, before it is sold.
about_author: Isandro Sterling is the pen name of a former architectural conservator who spent a decade documenting buildings slated for demolition. Their fiction explores how families inhabit spaces the way spaces inhabit them.

chapters.title: The Tuning Fork
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Tuning a dead woman's piano in a stranger's house, Lior hears the family's arguments still lodged in the floorboards. A letter arrives: Blackwood House is up for auction in six weeks. The beat is unease — the past has found a legal channel into the present.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Lior catalogs their own apartment — every object chosen to avoid meaning anything. Flashback fragments of childhood radiators clanking out the house's moods. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness, a life built as soundproofing.

chapters.title: Return to the Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Lior arrives early, before the siblings, and walks the derelict greenhouse their mother built. In its acoustics they hear an argument frozen mid-sentence from decades ago. Beat: vertigo of return; the house remembers more than anyone wants to.

chapters.title: Three Keys
chapters.summary: Sister Maren's POV. Maren, the executor, meets Lior at the house with brother Dev. Old roles snap back instantly — Maren manages, Dev deflects, Lior listens. Beat: friction disguised as efficiency; the auction is six weeks away and no one says why that terrifies them.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Know
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Working through the ground floor, Lior maps the house's heating system like a score and realizes the pipes were altered the same winter Father disappeared. Beat: first concrete clue that the family story has a structural flaw.

chapters.title: Mother, Present Tense
chapters.summary: Maren's POV at the care facility. Their mother, Odile, mistakes Maren for her own sister and speaks with startling clarity about 'the winter we don't discuss.' Then the clarity vanishes. Beat: grief braided with hope — memory surfaces only to sink again.

chapters.title: Dev's Version
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Over drinks, Dev offers his polished account of their father's departure: debts, another woman, clean exit. Lior notices Dev's hands shaking as he tells it. Beat: the official story performed too well to be true.

chapters.title: The Locked Piano Room
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. They find the music room sealed since childhood, key missing. Through the door, Lior tunes by ear and identifies a piano with a cracked soundboard — damaged deliberately, they suspect. Beat: dread sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Appraisal
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. An estate appraiser values the glasshouse contents; a buyer circles for the land itself. Maren must decide whether selling everything is mercy or betrayal. Beat: the price of survival becomes literal — acreage, lots, closing dates.

chapters.title: Odile's Recordings, Side One
chapters.summary: Lior finds reel-to-reel tapes hidden in the piano bench of the main parlor. Odile's young voice describes building the glasshouse 'so something in this family could grow without being watched.' Beat: tenderness and foreboding entwined.

chapters.title: The Winter We Don't Discuss
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. A neighbor's funeral draws the siblings together; an old family friend lets slip that Father didn't leave — he was made to leave. Beat: the arranged silence cracks audibly; each sibling suspects the others know more.

chapters.title: Cracked Soundboard
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior breaks into the music room and opens the piano: inside, taped beneath the frame, letters between Odile and someone unnamed — money, threats, a promise kept for thirty years. Beat: revelation as physical shock; the house was tuned to hide this.

chapters.title: Accusations in the Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Confronted with the letters, Dev erupts — the glasshouse becomes a courtroom. Old wounds reopen; Maren admits she helped pay Father off with Odile's inheritance. Beat: the family's careful architecture collapses under its own weight.

chapters.title: Side Two
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A second tape reveals Odile's bargain: she paid Father to go so he'd never touch the children, then built the glasshouse as penance and sanctuary. Beat: the mother reframed — protector, blackmailer, prisoner of her own arrangement.

chapters.title: Odile, Briefly Clear
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. During a lucid hour, Odile tells Maren she knows about the tapes and the auction: 'Sell the house. Keep the glasshouse. It's the only thing I built honestly.' Beat: blessing and burden handed over in a single sentence.

chapters.title: The Buyer
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The developer pushing the auction turns out to be connected to Father's old creditors — the sale would settle his debts at last, closing the circle. Beat: rising tension; survival's price may finally come due on the children.

chapters.title: What Each of Us Carried
chapters.summary: Three interleaved POVs (Lior, Maren, Dev) over one long night in the house. Each confesses what they did to survive childhood there — lies told, evidence burned, silences kept. Beat: catharsis without absolution; the inventory of unsaid things finally read aloud.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The auction proceeds lot by lot; the siblings watch their history itemized and sold. At the final call for the property itself, Maren stands — and asks for a recess. Beat: climax of nerve; the family intervenes in its own liquidation.

chapters.title: The Question
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. In front of the assembled bidders and family, Lior finally asks the question the whole family arranged itself around: not what happened to Father, but whether any of them could have survived staying — and whether Mother's price was worth their silence. Beat: raw, public reckoning; no easy answer, only truth.

chapters.title: Withdrawn
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Using pooled money and Odile's instruction, the siblings withdraw the glasshouse parcel from sale, letting the main house go. Dev pays a debt of his own by contacting Father — one phone call, unanswered. Beat: costly peace; some doors stay shut by choice.

chapters.title: Tuning the Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Alone in the saved glasshouse, Lior repairs the cracked piano and plays it for the first time; the room's acoustics hold every voice at once — mother, father, siblings, self. Beat: quiet transfiguration; identity no longer defined by what was hidden.

chapters.title: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Ensemble, final scene. Spring: the siblings plant the glasshouse together, Odile watching from a wheelchair, remembering nothing and smiling anyway. Lior keeps tuning pianos in other people's houses, but no longer keeps inventories. Beat: belonging redefined — not inherited, but tended.
